To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

older adults can improve their cognitive control after task-shifting-training and that this improvement is reflected in a redistribution of brain activation that is characterized by changes in spatio-temporal brain activation dynamics.

task-shifting training promotes proactive and reactive plasticity of transient brain activation and reduces the sustained activation of subcortical circuits, thereby improving behavioral performance in older adults.

training-induced neural changes are characterized by a redistribution of brain activation across frontoparietal and frontostriatal networks, with a particular focus on prefrontal regions, and a reconfiguration of the temporal dynamics of activation in fronto-striato-cortical networks, with a focus on transient activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and how cognitive-control training can improve brain activity in older adults.
the question whether and how the brain of older adults can change its functional activation patterns after task-shifting cognitive control training.
the question whether cognitive training can improve brain function in old age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
task shifting training promotes the redistribution of brain activation from fronto-parietally mediated transient mechanisms towards fronto-striatally mediated sustained mechanisms in old age.
task-shifting training is a promising intervention to counteract age-related deficits in cognitive control.

training induced a redistribution of brain activity from fronto-parieto-temporal to fronto-striato-temporal brain regions, which may reflect a more efficient and flexible recruitment of brain networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

task-shifting training promotes proactive changes in the brain that enable older adults to more efficiently maintain and bias task-set representations and reactive changes in the brain to more efficiently select responses.
task-shifting training promotes proactive and reactive changes in transient brain-activation mechanisms and overall reductions of sustained brain activation in older adults.

training-induced neural plasticity in old adults is characterized by a redistribution of transient brain activity in fronto-parieto-cortical and fronto-striat circuits, which in turn is associated with improved cognitive control performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is a highly flexible and adaptive system that can be trained to overcome age-related deficits.
the training-induced plasticity in the brain activation of older adults may reflect a reorganization of their brain networks to support the cognitive functions that are impaired in old age.

task-shifting training can promote proactive and reactive changes in transient brain-activation dynamics, and overall reductions of sustained brain activity, which in turn may enable older adults with preserved cognitive performance to reduce their reliance on compensatory mechanisms.
